items.text: Polycystic kidney disease occurs most frequently in Persian cats — an inherited disorder in which small, fluid-filled sacs develop in the kidney tissue over time.
items.attribution: Cornell Feline Health Center, Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine

items.text: Persian cats with polycystic kidney disease typically show increased thirst and urination, reduced appetite, weight loss, or lethargy — often first noticed around age seven.
items.attribution: Cornell Feline Health Center, Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine

items.text: Ultrasound is the only way to get a definitive diagnosis of polycystic kidney disease in a Persian cat — genetic testing alone can't determine how severe a case is.
items.attribution: Cornell Feline Health Center, Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine

items.text: A Persian cat suspected of carrying the polycystic kidney disease gene should be genetically tested, and a carrier should never be bred, to avoid passing the disease to kittens.
items.attribution: Cornell Feline Health Center, Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine

items.text: A Persian's large, protruding eyes have a reduced ability to close fully, leaving more of the eye's surface exposed — one reason Persians tear-stain more than most other breeds.
Many Persian cats develop brachycephalic obstructive airway syndrome — narrow nostrils, narrow nasal passages, and an overly long soft palate that can seriously restrict airflow.
A Persian's flattened face can leave the teeth misaligned (dental malocclusion), so they cannot bite and chew as effectively as a typically-shaped cat's jaw allows.
The deep facial skin folds common in Persian cats can predispose them to bacterial or fungal skin infections and facial dermatitis if not kept clean.
Long-haired breeds will need a little help, particularly Persians, who have a very thick undercoat and a long top layer of fur.
Persians and other long-coated breeds need regular cleaning underneath the tail, since fecal matter can stick to the fur there far more easily than on a short-haired cat.
As a Persian ages, reduced mobility can make self-grooming harder — many senior Persians need more hands-on brushing help than they did when younger.

"Their nasal openings are so small that they're basically breathing through a straw," one veterinary specialist has said of flat-faced cats — wheezing or snoring in a Persian is not just a normal breed trait, and is worth mentioning to your vet.
items.attribution: Humane World for Animals, formerly The Humane Society of the United States

items.text: Flat-faced cats like Persians struggle more to cool themselves in hot, humid weather, and air travel poses extra respiratory risk for the breed — keep them cool and avoid unnecessary heat exposure.
items.attribution: Humane World for Animals, formerly The Humane Society of the United States

items.text: A Persian that seems unusually low-energy may actually be struggling to breathe rather than simply being laid-back — reduced activity is worth mentioning to your vet rather than assuming it's just temperament.
items.attribution: Humane World for Animals, formerly The Humane Society of the United States
